flashcards.q: What is the Terraform state file, mechanically?
flashcards.a: A JSON mapping from each resource's configuration address to its provider-reported attributes as of the last refresh/apply — a cache of believed reality, not a live query.

flashcards.q: Why does terraform plan show unexpected changes even with no .tf edits made?
flashcards.a: Drift — plan refreshes tracked resources against real provider APIs before diffing (unless -refresh=false); the refresh caught a real-world change made outside Terraform, and the plan proposes reverting it to match config.

flashcards.q: What does state locking actually protect against, and what does it not?
flashcards.a: Protects against two concurrent applies writing state at the same time and corrupting it (S3 backend: separate DynamoDB lock table). Does NOT detect or prevent drift — a completely separate mechanism (the refresh step).

flashcards.q: A resource is renamed in config with no moved block. What does terraform plan show?
flashcards.a: The old address as destroy and the new address as create, even though it's conceptually the same resource with no real attribute changes — catastrophic for stateful resources.

flashcards.q: What does a moved block do, and how is it better than the old terraform state mv approach?
flashcards.a: Declares two addresses as the same underlying resource; plan then shows no destroy/create for it. Unlike state mv (an imperative CLI command run out-of-band, invisible in code review), moved blocks are declarative and reviewable in the same PR as the config change.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between built-in Terraform workspaces and separate dev/staging/prod environments?
flashcards.a: Built-in workspaces create multiple named state files from the SAME configuration, isolated only by state — good for identical parallel envs. Real environments with genuinely different config typically use separate backend configs per environment (or Terragrunt), not built-in workspaces.

flashcards.q: What's the over-abstraction trap with Terraform modules?
flashcards.a: A module built to cover every consumer's hypothetical use case upfront accumulates enough conditional logic and flags that using it correctly requires reading its internals — worse than extracting a smaller module from proven, real duplication across 2-3 teams.

flashcards.q: terraform test: difference between command=plan and command=apply modes?
flashcards.a: command=plan is fast, plan-only assertions with no real infrastructure created. command=apply genuinely provisions real infrastructure, asserts against real provider-returned attributes, then tears down — real cost and time per run.

flashcards.q: What is OpenTofu and why does it exist?
flashcards.a: A Linux Foundation-hosted, genuinely open-source fork of Terraform created after HashiCorp's 2023 BSL license change, drop-in compatible through roughly the 1.5.x line and diverging since. Real, live, production-used, not a footnote.

flashcards.q: Where does Terraform/HCL genuinely lose to Pulumi/CDK, and where does it genuinely win?
flashcards.a: Loses on complex, loop/conditional-heavy infra logic and native unit testing (Pulumi/CDK use real programming languages). Wins on provider/module ecosystem breadth and a simple, shared declarative vocabulary across a whole team.

flashcards.q: Why should CI apply the exact saved .tfplan artifact rather than re-running plan+apply fresh after merge?
flashcards.a: Re-running plan fresh after merge can compute a different plan than what was reviewed (a TOCTOU gap) if anything changed in the interim. Applying the saved artifact guarantees what's applied is exactly what a human approved.

flashcards.q: Why does terraform plan get slow on a monolithic 400-resource root module even for a one-line change?
flashcards.a: Plan refreshes ALL tracked resources against real provider APIs before diffing, regardless of the change's size. Fix: split state along logical/lifecycle boundaries (networking, data, app tier) into separate root modules/backends.
